name: Vitamin D deficiency
definition: A shortage of vitamin D in the body, which can weaken bones and muscles over time.
overview: Vitamin D deficiency means the body does not have enough vitamin D. The skin makes it from summer sunlight, and food supplies only a small share, so in the UK autumn and winter sunlight is too weak to meet needs. Many people have no symptoms or only vague ones such as tiredness and aches. Prolonged or severe deficiency can affect the bones and muscles, causing rickets in children and osteomalacia in adults.
causes: Too little vitamin D taken in from food
Conditions that limit absorption, such as malabsorption syndromes
riskFactors: Rarely going outdoors, living in a care home or usually covering most skin outside
Infants and young children, especially breastfed babies
Crohn's disease, coeliac disease or ulcerative colitis
signs: Bowed legs in children with rickets
complications: Low blood calcium, very rarely with cramps and seizures
diagnosis: Diagnosis is usually by a blood test for 25-hydroxyvitamin D, requested when symptoms or risk factors suggest it. Experts do not fully agree on the level that counts as deficient, and routine testing of people without symptoms is not recommended. If osteomalacia is suspected, bone-related blood tests and sometimes an X-ray are used.
treatment: Treatment usually involves vitamin D supplements, with diet and sensible sun exposure, often an initial higher-dose course followed by a daily maintenance supplement, then follow-up to confirm correction and check for toxicity.
prevention: The NHS advises that everyone should consider a daily vitamin D supplement during the autumn and winter, with some groups advised to take one all year. Skin should still be protected from sunburn.
seekCare: Contact a GP for a routine appointment about persistent bone pain, muscle weakness or aches, or a child with bowed legs. Contact NHS 111 or the GP the same day for new unexplained muscle cramps. Call 999 for a seizure.

sections.heading: What is vitamin D deficiency and how does the body get vitamin D?
sections.body:
Vitamin D deficiency means the body does not have enough vitamin D. The skin makes vitamin D from summer sunlight, and in the UK sunlight is not strong enough in the autumn and winter to make enough. Food supplies only a small share of the vitamin D most people need.

Oily fish, egg yolks, red meat, and fortified cereals and spreads are the main food sources. Two common drivers of deficiency are a low intake of foods containing vitamin D and reduced time in the sun. Clinicians do not fully agree on the blood level that should count as deficient, and different guidelines give different definitions.

Many people with low vitamin D have no symptoms, or only vague ones. For this reason the problem is often found only when a doctor has a reason to look for it.

sections.heading: What are the symptoms of vitamin D deficiency?
sections.body:
Vague symptoms such as tiredness and general aches are the most common picture. In adults, prolonged or severe deficiency can cause bone pain, joint pain, muscle pain, fatigue, muscle twitching and weakness. Because these symptoms are unspecific and very common, clinicians can over-suspect the condition.

Osteomalacia, a softening of the bones in adults, is the adult bone disease most clearly linked to vitamin D deficiency, and it causes weak bones, bone pain and muscle weakness. UK guidance lists muscle aches and weakness, especially in the thigh and buttock muscles, a waddling walk, and long-lasting widespread pain.

In children, the equivalent bone condition is rickets, which can cause bowed legs, bone pain, muscle weakness and a waddling walk. Children with deficiency may also be irritable or lethargic, have delayed development, bone changes or fractures. Very rarely, low calcium linked to the problem can cause cramps and seizures.

sections.heading: What causes vitamin D deficiency and who is more likely to get it?
sections.body:
Deficiency tends to arise when too little vitamin D is taken in, too little is made by the skin, or the body cannot absorb or use it well. Other factors named in medical reviews include darker skin, malabsorption syndromes, some medicines such as corticosteroids, ageing, smoking, obesity, and liver or kidney disease.

The NHS says people who rarely go outdoors, live in a care home or usually cover most of their skin outside are less likely to make enough vitamin D from sunlight. People with dark skin, such as those of African, African-Caribbean or South Asian background, may also make less vitamin D from sunlight. NICE public health work on prevention also names infants and young children, pregnant and breastfeeding women, and people over 65.

The US National Institutes of Health notes that breastfed infants, people with conditions that limit fat absorption such as Crohn's disease, coeliac disease or ulcerative colitis, and people who have had certain operations are more likely to have trouble getting enough.

sections.heading: How is vitamin D deficiency diagnosed?
sections.body:
Vitamin D status is measured with a blood test for 25-hydroxyvitamin D, the most stable form of the vitamin. A GP may arrange a blood test for vitamin D and calcium if a person has symptoms or risk factors. NICE CKS says testing everyone is not recommended; testing is advised when musculoskeletal symptoms may be due to low vitamin D or there is a clinical reason, such as a recent fall.

If osteomalacia is suspected, doctors may also check blood calcium, phosphate and alkaline phosphatase, sometimes parathyroid hormone, and may arrange an X-ray of the painful area. A low vitamin D result alone does not establish osteomalacia, which is defined by abnormal bone-related blood results.

sections.heading: How is vitamin D deficiency treated and prevented?
sections.body:
Treatment usually involves vitamin D supplements, together with attention to diet and sensible sun exposure. NICE CKS describes an initial period of higher-dose vitamin D followed by a lower daily maintenance supplement. Follow-up is used to confirm that levels have corrected and to watch for toxicity, which usually shows as a high blood calcium.

The NHS advises that everyone should consider a daily vitamin D supplement during the autumn and winter, and some groups are advised to take one all year. Taking too much over a long time can raise calcium in the blood, which may weaken bones and damage the kidneys and heart. Sunlight cannot cause vitamin D overdose, but skin still needs protection from sunburn and skin cancer.

sections.heading: When should you see a doctor about low vitamin D?
sections.body:
A routine GP appointment is the usual route for persistent bone pain, muscle weakness or aches, or for a child with bowed legs. A GP can arrange a blood test and decide whether treatment is needed. Persistent musculoskeletal pain can lead to referral or specialist advice when it does not have a clear cause. Call NHS 111 or contact the GP the same day for muscle cramps or spasms that are new and unexplained. Call 999 for a seizure.

People who think they are at higher risk can ask the GP or pharmacist whether a supplement is suitable for them. Supplements should not be taken in excess, because too much can raise blood calcium. Clinicians also take care with supplementation to avoid adverse effects, which is one reason follow-up matters.

faqs.q: Can vitamin D deficiency be corrected?
faqs.a: Treatment usually aims to restore vitamin D with supplements, alongside diet and sun exposure. Follow-up checks whether levels have corrected and whether any toxicity has developed. Whether symptoms such as bone pain improve depends on the person and the cause, and a GP can advise.

faqs.q: Does low vitamin D make you tired?
faqs.a: Tiredness is one of the vague symptoms the NHS lists, but many people with low vitamin D have no symptoms. Because tiredness is very common and unspecific, it does not on its own show that vitamin D is low. A GP can look for other causes.

faqs.q: Can you get enough vitamin D from sunlight in the UK?
faqs.a: In the summer months the skin can make vitamin D from sunlight. In the autumn and winter, UK sunlight is not strong enough to make enough. The NHS advises everyone to consider a daily supplement during those seasons, and some people are advised to take one all year. Skin still needs protection from sunburn.

faqs.q: Can you take too much vitamin D?
faqs.a: Yes, over a long period too much can raise calcium in the blood, which may weaken bones and damage the kidneys and heart. Sunlight does not cause overdose. The NHS gives upper limits for supplements, so a pharmacist or GP can advise on suitable products.

faqs.q: Who should have a vitamin D blood test?
faqs.a: NICE CKS says testing everyone is not recommended. It advises testing when muscle or bone symptoms may be due to low vitamin D, or when there is another clinical reason such as a recent fall. The decision is made by the clinician.

faqs.q: What is the difference between rickets and osteomalacia?
faqs.a: Rickets is the childhood form of bone softening linked to low vitamin D, and osteomalacia is the adult form. Rickets can cause bowed legs, while osteomalacia brings bone pain and muscle weakness. A GP can arrange tests if either is suspected.
